blocks.x: Now I think we got it going. Let's see, this is Rio 1, November 8th, 1962 at 1821 6th Street.
And give your name again. Edward Johnson Sr. And what do they call you again? Professional name, Big Head Eddie Johnson.
I see. Let's play a little bit back and then we can see how it's going.
Sounds good. Now where were you born? In Baton Rouge. And what was the date again? November 2nd, 1903.
And did you play with many bands around there? Did you move to the city when you were young or what? Oh no, I was done.

I moved in the morning. First band I played with with the Olympia band. I played quite a job with the Duxedo band, fumes and parades. And also played an enormous choir down at Old Ebsen House. And then played with the Jitney Dance Hall. Jitney Dance Hall? Old Ebsen House?
Yeah. They were born at that time at the Palace Dance Hall.
But it was in Old Ebsen House Billings. And it was every night. And such musicians was Arnold McGuire, several other children. And all.
What about Baton Rouge? Do you remember anything from there?

Oh, I wasn't playing music then. I remember some of the musicians. Just Tiff Johnson. No relation to me though. And Guy Kelly. After was he grown up, he came to New Orleans and played with the Tuxedo band during the time that I was playing.
Did the bands in Baton Rouge sound anything like the bands down here?

Well, during that time, jazz was really good. Bands around Baton Rouge such as Professor Claiborne Williams and Knox and Tiff Johnson bands. There were about only three bands at that time doing Baton Rouge. Who was Knox? Knox was the drum. With the Tiff Johnson band. It was a long time before I was playing music then. I wasn't playing music then. In fact, I didn't play any music in Baton Rouge at all. I only started playing music since I came to New Orleans.
Was Guy Kelly playing when you were living in Baton Rouge?
Yes, he was playing, but not... Yeah, he was playing in the band in Baton Rouge, yeah.
Is he about your age, a little older?
No, I think if he... Well, he's dead now. Yeah. If he had been living, he would have been around my age. He died in Chicago, I think.
How old were you when you left Baton Rouge? I was quite a little bit. Teenage. Teenage. Yeah. So Guy Kelly started pretty young, wasn't he? Yes, he did. Did you take lessons in Baton Rouge? No, no.
Right here in the one from Ball Bonds. From Ball Bonds?

Yeah, that's my first lessons. Mm-hmm. What instrument? Oh, saxophone. Altho, a tenor? Altho. You always talk to Altho? I always talk to Altho and I played tenor, but Papa Sutherstein, soprano. Let's go back to the bands you, the very first bands you played with here.
The first band I played with was on all the past, I think. One empty band. One empty game, man.
I've met his wife and his son, his daughter, but I never met him, of course.
I hope he won't be, because he's dead. I know.

Well, I think he was dead before I ever came to this. Oh, yes, yes, yes. He's been dead a while. Yeah. What about that band? What kind of band would you describe that? Oh, we had a wonderful jazz band.

We had a seven-piece jazz band. It was very good. At one time we were working every night. That's what I did for about four or six months. Every night of the week we were working. Different places every night? Different places every night.
That's quite a feat to do that.
Yes, at that time we didn't have as many bands as we got now either.
Well, who was in the band?

We had such bands as Talbot, Talbot, and Benny, who was on the band. He was on bamboo. Every guy named Erter Franz was on piano. And I was on bamboo… I mean… Siphon… Reese professe was on bamboo… And, uh, El Basin, I don't understand. Who's, who's the other one? Trombone? Oh, yes, we have Trombone. Uh, Roberson, Tim Roberson. Oh, yeah. And Ike.
Oh, Ike Roberson. Did you read many numbers of that band?
Well, quite a few. It wasn't a reading band, but we had reading some time.
Where would you get the arrangements to read from?
Well, sometimes El Phon's people would write them first. Simple arrangements, it was smaller things, wasn't nothing too hard. I wanted courses.
Would you buy stock arrangements at one?
Oh, yeah.
Stocks and, uh...
And he used to write some simple things for us.
Uh-huh. I wanted to know. How would he arrange? I mean, would it be a lot of... You said just choruses?
Oh, yeah, introductions and first and second choruses.
Uh-huh. I see. Well, would it be a... You'd have a different part for the different saxophones? Oh, yeah, yes, yes, yes.

Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Would it be... We had the alto and tenor, the alto and tenor, and the trombone and piano and trumpet, of course. That would be the most fun, but the rest of them would just fit in. That'd be good.
Oh, yeah. But I mean, would the saxophones play in harmony with the trumpet and trombone, or would they... Oh, yeah, they would play harmony, you know what I said?
Three-part harmonies.
Three-part harmonies, yeah. They'd blend them like that, is what I'm getting at. Three-part harmonies.
Uh-huh.

I see. Well, that would sound nice, I'd play. Oh, yeah. Good. It sounded really good. A lot of stuff like that. And then you could get off, too. Oh, yeah. It had to be in it. Uh-huh. About what year was that? Oh, that was on 1926, I think.
26, 27. That's when you first started, right?
Yeah. Were they playing a lot of solos then, or would you... Yeah. Yeah. That's when you first started, right?
26, 27. I think. 26, I think. 26 and 27. Yeah. Were they playing a lot of solos then, or would you... play ensemble, or how would they work?
Well, the naturally solo, different parts, different men would take solos and then we'd play harmony underneath them. Uh-huh. You wouldn't take down up then much, huh?
Oh, yes.

We'd take a chorus, and then the main chorus or two, and then the piano would take one, we'd drop in the trumpet, and we'd play the gentle cytoine and the alto with the harmonies, play underneath the trumpet, whatever instrument that would play in the melody.
Oh, yeah. That's a good thing to help the other guys out. I always help the bands a lot. I like to hear that. It gives it that full sound. Yeah.
And the introduction note would be playing, but naturally though, we'd be playing at all times. And then the last chorus would be dropped, and we'd go forward and be loud. Oh, yeah.
Well, would you play the introduction loud or solos?
Oh, yeah. Introduction... All the introduction have to be loud, then come down and solos playing the melodies.
Introduction loud, the first chorus is solos. Yeah.
And the last chorus is going up, and it's like our final chorus would be loud. Oh, I understand.
What would be some of the numbers that you play? Do you remember any of the tunes that were popping on those? Oh, yeah.

Tisket or Tisket, and Heeby Jeeby, and the apple tree, and all such numbers like that in older times. Three o'clock in the morning, there's walls that we feature that. And sometimes, that's a number, no walls, sometimes. Yeah. They exactly teach you that too.

How does sometime go? What does it like? What is it like? I often wondered, did you play many waltzes then? About how many numbers out of a night? Say would every third number be a waltz, every fourth number?
No, no, I guess whenever we feel like it, there wouldn't be no such set up as three or four numbers at a time. At a time we would play about four or five waltzes.
All in a row?
No, no.
During the course of the evening. Would you play long hours then?
Oh yes, during the time from eight to two, to three. It would be five or six hours in the season.
Not too different from the harmony end.
No, no. Thanks, Johnny.
Did you have anybody that you really admired a lot when you were growing up in those days? Any musician that you looked up to as an ideal?
Yes. Paul Barnes, Bonnie Begarde.
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.
Yeah. He was a saxophone player, and saxophone player, yeah. Uh-huh. Yeah, that was it. Paul Barnes and Bonnie Begarde is my two favorite musicians.
And where did Bonnie Begarde play then? Where he's playing now?
Then, then those days. Oh, then. On what instruments? Oh, he was playing ground-head. Mostly ground-head, yeah. Yeah, he was a stickler ground-head. At that time, I think he was playing a few songs.
Well, I know he could play saxophones too when he had to.

That's a good point, mm-hmm. I've heard he won records on saxophone with Ken Lava, huh? Yeah. What was Paul Barnes playing then? Mostly alto. Mostly alto. I know he's a good clarinet player today, too. Yeah.

Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland Oakland
But three other fellows from New Orleans. We get to the Johnnison, Paul Gorns, and Cythron, Oklahoma, Mike DeLay, and Trump.
Did you know Mike DeLay down here?
He worked with us sometimes.
Oh yeah? Which band was this?
Yeah, at the Epstein House when I was on the gym and dance. Oh. And when a normal twig was sick, he didn't make it, Mike DeLay would make it.
What kind of trumpet player was Montoya? With who? What kind of trumpet player was Arnold Montoya?

Oh he was a standard good first class musician. He was. He could play good. He could take a mouthpiece alone with a glass and get his on playing the trumpet. And some of his control he had with his lips, you know what I mean? He played really good.
Well did he play mostly by note or? Oh yeah.
He was a speaker of the music band. He came up in the circus. He had a triple tone, flutter tone. Most of you musicians can do nowadays. He could take a horn and all that. He'd do everything.

Did he ever play much cut bucket music? Yes. He could do that too? He could do that too, yes. What about somebody like Manuel Perez? Was he a cut bucket? Yes, Manuel Perez was another good man too. He could, I know he could read good. Oh yeah. I just didn't know if he ever played much cut bucket stuff or what. Oh yes. He could do both. He also could read.
He was a good street man, played parades and funerals. He was a good man. Yeah.
Well they're bringing the Onward band back now.
I know he's.
Uh huh. That should be good. Maybe there'll be more work. I hope so. We were at the parade Saturday. Up at Tulane.
Oh yes, yes, yes.
The Onward band was up there. The first job out.
Yes.
The very first one. But you used to play in brass bands then too you said? Right at that.
Uh huh.
I played the Ripper band. Most of the Tuxedo band. Now which Tuxedo is that? Papa Saris Band. The original.
Yeah. And I also played in the Tulane brass band that L.C. Landry was later. He's dead now.
Uh huh. Who was in the Tulane in the day?

Mm-hm. Who had such men as Dalkywall Warner and Dalkywall. and Landry, a few of them, I can't think of just young. Some of them were practically old, nearly all of them were dead. Rodgers was playing drums.
I knew him well. Ernest Rodgers, you talking about? Yeah. He was a good straight drummer, and beat going.
All those were straight men, you know, parade men, see, parade a few men. Uh-huh. At that time, sometimes I saw myself play two films a day.
Two a day, huh?
And, really good. Now I don't play any more brass bands, anyway.
No? Why did you give that up?
Well, authorize, get more, nothing now but to sit down now. Yeah.
Well, that's hard enough. Oh, yes. Those long hours and everything. Uh-huh. Did they have many organizations then? Societies? Oh, yes, quite a few.
Clubs? Oh, yes. What are some of them that you work for? Oh, Tulane, the 80-30 Club, and, uh, the Valets, the Zulus, I played quite a few of them.
There must have been so many of them you can't remember.
And they all just went down. Yeah. It used to be all about six, six, six. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. The fact that it's not the brass bands, not like it was, you know, I mean, I don't want them like they used to be.
You liked them better than the old times, huh? Well, yeah. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. So, my son would much rather play a funeral parade than me. Uh-huh. Well, that's marvelous music.
I think it is. They had all such good drummers, those things. Who was some of the other favorite musicians? Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. What other favorite musicians you like, you know, other than saxophone players?
Ernest Rapania on drums. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And, uh, George McCollum, trumpet. Did you work much with him? Oh, yes. We're a WPA band. We've worked together for quite a few years. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
I guess you're in those pictures of the WPA band. I've seen several different ones.
Uh-huh. Every one of them.
You played with them from the beginning? Uh-huh.
I played with them. The band started off in a hundred and some hour and got 135 men and ended up with 35. And I happened to be around in the 35 group.
Oh, yeah.
Of course I played an odd instrument. I played barricade on saxophone. Oh.
In those days, huh? Uh-huh.
I still have my barricade on saxophone. Uh-huh. That's a good instrument.

I never hear that around much. No, I know. Except in big bands, once in a while you'll catch one. I know a few fellas that play with big bands. Well, uh, did you play baritone in the street much? No, no.
Had no time. Uh-huh. On an altone.
Never soprano or tenor or barricade?
Nothing but altone street.
Did you ever fool around with clarinet, by the way? At all?
Yes, very, never been that much. I don't know, for some reason, uh, I didn't like it. I was still in all that. I'd known there would have been such a demand for it. But now, you know, stuck with it.
Wow. Well, it seems to be the instrument now. It seems like so many of the clarinet players died off all of a sudden. Yeah. That's a real shame.
Yeah, we don't have a, but a few clarinet players. Yeah.

Well, I don't have quit. It's still alive. Like, Mealy Barnes never plays anymore. No. He says his mouth is all corroded. Yes, ma'am. That's his word for it. All corroded. I was both corroded. The first time I was ever there. Yeah, that's what he said.
I can't blame my mouth's all corroded. Who was in that old tuxedo, Brad's family, those days? Oh, we can't doubt.
Happy Goldstein. Mm-hmm. And, uh, Ernest Reppens. And, uh, Ernest Reppens. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I remember we had John Porter.
Oh yeah. What was he playing? Bass. Bass. I know he played a lot of instruments.
Oh yeah. He died. He was on the phone and stuff like that. I was with him the day he died.
Yeah, that was right. It really was a shock. I remember he was on the main. Let's see. Did the band have trombones in them? Oh yeah. They were like that.
The trombone players. They played Rekha. I don't know. I don't know. I think it was the other way. I still fall back. Oh yeah.
Well, it'll come to you. And I didn't understand about the tuxedo. I never got straight. Did the same guys play in the brass band? They played in the dance band then?
Sometimes, yeah. No. No. No. No.
Now you had a clarinet play in the brass band you said? Yes.
And did you have a tenor player? No. Tenor player, not the brass band.
No, I see. So, I guess sometimes they wouldn't play in both bands. They had a big sax actually. They called Paul Bonds.
He was the feature man in the brass band also, in the barate band. And the dance band.

Did they have two altos sometimes you played with them? Yeah, sometimes they had two altos in the tenor. Oh, and the dance band. But Paul Bonds didn't play in the street much, huh? Yes, he played alto. He played alto sometimes. Oh, I see. I got the street. When did you play with the Eureka recently or years ago? Oh, years ago.

Oh, I met about Eureka about last, seven years ago. I played the Eureka. But I wasn't considered a member of the band at that time. I just was fiddling, pain-ditting. Somebody couldn't make it such as Harold. You know, couldn't make it. He'd send me in his place. Yeah, Roddy was with him for a long time. Yeah, Roddy was beginning to get sick. I would go in his place.
How's Happy Goldson doing?
Pretty nice, I heard him. He still walked with him. You haven't? He's sick. I haven't seen him in quite a while. That's what I heard in the news for them.

I haven't seen him in quite a while. I just, you know, I try to get him out of the scene, but... So many people have been sick lately. And Buster Moore lives up around here somewhere, too, doesn't he? You know him? Who is that? Buster Moore, trombone player?
Oh, yes, yes, yes.
I hear he's been sick, too.
Yeah. And trombone player.
Yeah. Left-handed. Yeah, that's strange to see. I looked funny when you see that.
Trombone player, left-handed.
Did you ever know Sonny Henry? I certainly did.
Do you remember him personally? He was in the WPA band with us.
Oh. And you ever worked with him in the other band? Oh, yes, we worked with him. The Aretha, too. Yeah. I thought maybe you worked with him early or something. I'm trying to remember.
I'm doing the WPA days in the WPA band.
Did the WPA make any records of that band? No, no, no, no, no, no, no.
That's a shame. It's such a big band. Well, even playing for nothing is possible to you. There's a band that is working. It's playing for charity because we're going to steal the speech.
I thought they made a movie or something.
No. I don't remember.

That's funny. I got that confused. Montague told me about somebody making a movie. Sidney Montague and having to play St. Louis Blues over and over again. I thought it was a WPA band on the city park, but I guess I got it confused with somebody else. Have you ever made any records any other time? No.
No.

And so many of the bands you played with have made records. That's what I did. You just missed that break. That's right. And now there's more interest and it looks like more companies are coming down here making records. Maybe your time will come.
Almost probably.
Well, how long have you led your own band now?

Oh well off the dawn, say for instance I'm down at the Home and Inn now for about eight years. And at the Palace Dance Hall I worked there for two years as a manager there. That's about the only two bands I had in our leadership.
You were leading that band with Matoya? No, I'm in the twine. Matoya? No, no. Oh no, another time. I see. I'm in managing. Who was in that band with Matoya?
David Jones and Tim and myself on the outro. William Foster playing the banjo.
Uh-huh.
And Milford over there playing piano. Uh-huh. David.
I think of it now.
Come on.
Oh yeah, Henry Russell's playing drums. Oh yeah.

What happened to Davy Jones anyway? Oh he's out west someplace. He's out in California like the time I was there. He seems to have disappeared that day. I guess I could find him if I ever get out that way.
He probably sees Paul Barnes. Yes.
You remember him? I never knew him. You never knew him? He's a little before my time I guess. I've been living here for thirteen years now.

Oh yeah, that was before your time. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. He was a wonderful man, wonderful musician dear. That's what everyone says. Great teacher. Very well. 13 years now. Oh yeah, that was before your time.
He was a wonderful man, wonderful musician, Jim.
That's what everyone says.

He was a great teacher. He played well. He was a man that could play soprano and the sweetest tone you ever heard. Marinet soprano, melliform, piano sites, no trumpet, he'd play everything and teach them all.
That's what Streckfus still talks about him, Captain Vern Streckfus.
Oh yeah, yeah, he was on the boat.
Telling about melliform, what a different tone he gave and all that. Who was in your band at the Palace Dance Hall?
That's what I just did, Matoya and David Jones.
Oh, that was your band. Matoya was a leader? Yeah. And you were the manager. I see. Well, did that band play the same kind of music you played at the Home of the Inn?
No, the same kind of music like we're doing now, the Dixie Man. In fact, I always was a Dixie Man there. I see.
But you can play the stock arrangements? Oh yes, yes. I can read music. You can play any kind of dance music. Any kind of music. Either way.
I can transpose a bit, arrange a bit.
Who have you done arrangements for? No, no, just model outfits. For your little outfits, I see. You like that?
Oh yes, quite interesting.
Yeah, it's fun to do things like that. Yeah.
Especially if you get working with a bunch of fellows that's agreeable. It is nice to have new things.
There must be some differences in the music now than what happened years ago. I mean, when I go down to the Home of the Inn, you must play some things different now.

Well, it is. Because the swing is kind of different. As on the light of the air, you get your drummer that can't play the real full rhythm. The whole band is based upon the drummer and the piano. You know what you see what I mean? And if they had got a beat foot, they would throw the band off. But in those days, the drummers really were good. They were really good honestly. The seasoned drummers that were really good play. They have a few of them right now, the drummers really. Good.
Well, you like a strong bass drum beat. Absolutely.
It weighs about a full foot beat. I guess the dancers like it too.
Oh yeah. They want to hear that beat. That helps them along. Sure. What kind of dances do they do now that they didn't do then? Way back.

So, nowadays that they didn't do in the old days? Yeah. So, here's the Mambo, they didn't do that. Remember what old days? Yeah. The Mambo didn't do that in the old days. No. That's what I can think of right now. The only general, the old time, there was waltz. See, if a band couldn't play a waltz, or a shout-out, we didn't have a job. You played shout-out since then? Oh yes. But not down there, no one had. No. I played shout-out down there, they were standing there. They couldn't do it on the plane anymore. Well, how did the shout-out go? Well, it's a different tempo than the ordinary four foot is. Could you beat it off with your foot there? I think we can pick it up. No, I don't think I can. You don't remember it. No. The drum was up there. See? And strong, little ones. Yeah. Do you remember the names of any of their dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
You remember the shot issues you played?
Yeah, I think I remember one. Three of Black Berries. That was one that I played.
I don't know, I think about that. You can't play to the mother, dear? No, no, no. That's probably sheet music for her around, something like that. We'll run across it.
Yeah. She's got a job with her nipples in the vocal theater. They come out in the sets. She's got a job with her nipples.
Did you play many rags back in those days?
Oh yeah. Tiger rags. High society nights that was your standard. You know what I mean?
It was really good. Did you play many Joplin nipples, you said? No, no. Not too much. Not too many of them. I see. What about the twist back in those days? Did they do the twist?

No, no. It wasn't the same thing as the twist in those days. The twist was a brand new something that did come up last two years, a year and a half, and one over like a whole soul fight. It was all good.

Do you think the twist is helping music or hurting it or what? No, I think it's helping it. I guess things like that. I'd always put some more people out there and more demand for a lot of music. Something like that helps. I think this is about to run out. We can put another one on, okay? Okay? . . .

This is Reel 2. Whoa, whoa, that's going. Reel 2. Uh, Eddie Johnson. And, uh, it's November the 8th, 1962. Jack, you want to put your name on here so the secretary will know who it is? This will be, uh, Jack Hurley. Yeah, and my name's Dick Allen. Got to do that before. We were talking about banjos. What kind of banjos did you use?
In the, in the orchestra's? Mm-hmm. Six-string banjos.

Did you say that you also sometimes used the five-string? The five-string, yeah. Now, was that five-string banjo tuned like it is now with the drum string on the top? Yes, uh-huh. How, was the six-string banjo then tuned like a guitar? Like a guitar, yes. The same fingering as a guitar. Did it use a gut string or a? Or would it use, no, no, no, steel, steel.

Steel. Steel. Metal on the board. See, the, uh, guitar banjo is the same fingering as a guitar, as I said before. Physicians were the same. But it just gave you that tone for the banjo. Yeah. That, uh, stretch-headed tone. Yeah.
That's interesting. Did your band ever use any, did you ever do any breakdown? Oh, yeah. Mm-hmm.
You'd have to have a banjo for that? Oh, yeah. Banjos are a thing. Banjos and bass, violins, and, uh, clarinets, standard instruments of all the musicians.
Small bands and band, big bands. By what time did the four-string banjo come in and start replacing these old types?
Oh, back in the day, you see, around, let's see, about 19, 1935, 1903.
Around, 1930. About when the big bands started coming in, did the big bands sound? Yeah, they were using bands, everything.

Mm-hmm. Johnny St. Cyr still uses a six-string. Really? Oh, yeah. Yeah, he still uses it. He's got one out of Disneyland, huh? Never run into that. Well, you'll see him. I'll show you some pictures of him. Yeah. All right. Why don't you sit here and watch it? Because I'm afraid my voice is a little loud from here. He just swaps. He plays, uh, he used to play with William Strong, too, at the time. He was strong. Yeah.
He gets all band jobs. We've got some wonderful records with him on. Yeah.

Did you ever, uh, use the 12-string guitar? Oh, no. No. Uh-uh. The 12 and the 16-string guitar is known as the harp guitar. Right. Yeah, but they don't use the harp guitar. That's the lead-belly style. Yeah. They'll use that in style, mostly.

Mm-hmm. I wanted to ask you about some of the people that have played with you at the Harmony Inn. I know a lot of them have been down there from time to time. Mm-hmm. Who were some of the musicians that have been down there? Nowadays or before? Well, we talked about, let's see, well, nowadays. Who's with you right now?

I wanted to have Anderson on trumpet. Mm-hmm. And Big Art drums. And, uh, beginning Tomorrow Night with Smitty on piano. So. Before then, we'd have such men as, uh, as, uh, Willie Paiju, a trumpet. Edgar Smith on drums. And, uh, I forgot about the name of, Ramsey. Oh, Lindsey Ramsey, yeah. Yeah. He was playing piano. Mm-hmm. What happened to him? Well, he decided to quit. I guess he, as, uh, immediately said he had what? In the mouth?
Maybe he said he got corroded. His mouth was all corroded.
He, he, he must got corroded the fingers because he quit playing. Yeah. He quit playing.
And Tommy. Yeah, well. I never have seen him with anybody else. Did he play with any other bands? No. No. No. Mostly with you through the ears? Mm-hmm. Where does he live in here?
